query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high-entropy alloy, intrinsic brittle behavior can emerge via a dynamic process in which extreme, deformation-induced grain refinement leads to an ultra‐nanocrystalline surface (or sub‐surface) layer that, even in the absence of impurity segregation or intermetallic precipitation, has reduced grain boundary cohesion. This reduced cohesion promotes cavitation (nanoporosity) at high-angle boundaries and triple junctions under high-strain rate or low-friction sliding conditions, ultimately manifesting as toughness degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially coarse- or moderately coarse-grained, single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., the well-studied CoCrFeMnNi) with a stable solid solution structure and no visible grain-boundary segregation or intermetallic precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled sliding or high strain-rate deformation tests in an inert or ultra-high vacuum environment to stimulate dynamic grain refinement. In a controlled comparison, pre-annealed samples with intentionally coarser grains (to suppress extreme refinement) would be tested alongside samples expected to dynamically refine to the ultra-nanocrystalline state.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under high-strain rate or sliding contact conditions in inert/UHV atmospheres (minimizing thermal segregation and oxidation), with tests conducted at ambient to moderately elevated temperatures where dynamic amorphization is expected to be activated.
generation.structural_mediator: Ultra-fine (10–50 nm) grains and the grain boundaries within the dynamically refined surface layers, including triple junctions where local stress concentration can lead to nanocavitation.
generation.mechanism: Under severe shear, the initially coarse-grained HEA dynamically refines near its contact surface via a process akin to dynamic recrystallization/amorphization. When the refined grain size falls below a critical threshold, the traditional dislocation-mediated plasticity is suppressed in favor of grain-boundary sliding. This results in local weakening due to reduced grain boundary cohesion, leading to cavitation and premature brittle failure—a mechanism distinct from conventional grain-boundary embrittlement via impurity segregation or intermetallic precipitation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline material (which retains a coarser, more ductile grain structure), samples that develop an ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer under high strain rates will exhibit lower toughness, increased wear particle generation from cavitation events, and a brittle fracture mode with intergranular crack propagation. The controlled comparison sample with pre-coarser grains (reducing dynamic refinement) should show higher toughness and less evidence of nanoporosity-induced decohesion.
generation.baseline: An initially single-phase, coarse-grained HEA without significant dynamic grain refinement (and therefore without the cavitation-induced grain boundary decohesion mechanism), which conventionally is expected to maintain toughness provided there is no segregation or intermetallic formation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to be relevant for service conditions involving high strain rates and low friction (e.g., sliding wear or high-rate deformation) in environments that minimize chemical effects (no oxidation/segregation). It may not apply in regimes dominated by conventional segregation-induced embrittlement or in low strain-rate conditions where dynamic refinement is absent.
generation.uncertainty: While the dynamic grain refinement and associated cavitation mechanism have precedent in observations of inverse Hall-Petch behavior in HEAs, the precise critical grain size and the extent to which nanocavitation alone degrades toughness (without any minor chemical effects) require further quantification. There is uncertainty regarding the universality of this effect across different compositionally complex alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same single-phase HEA. One set is left untreated (allowing dynamic grain refinement to occur under high strain rate sliding tests), and the other is pre-annealed to establish a stable, coarser surface microstructure that resists further refinement. Subject both sets to identical high strain-rate sliding or shear tests in an inert (UHV) environment while monitoring surface microstructure evolution in situ via high-resolution TEM or STEM. Mechanical properties, fracture toughness, and wear particle formation will be quantitatively compared.
measurements: Grain size distribution at the deformed surface (via TEM/STEM)
Friction coefficient and wear rate (tribological testing)
Fracture toughness and ductility from mechanical tests
Microscopic evidence of cavitation (nanoporosity) along grain boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If pre-annealed, coarser-grained samples (which suppress dynamic grain refinement) exhibit the same degree of toughness degradation and brittle fracture behavior as the untreated samples, then the hypothesis that dynamic refinement-induced nanocavitation drives brittleness in single-phase HEAs is falsified. Conversely, if only the samples that dynamically refine to ultra-nanocrystalline structures display brittle behavior and nanocavitation features, then the hypothesis is supported.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

This calculation leads to a prediction for the average high angle grain boundary energy (at 300 K), γHAGB,calc≅0.87Jm2. Although recent experimental measurements of HAGB energy with this same alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) exist, a comparison of this prediction is difficult. Measurements of grain boundary energy are sensitive to thermally-driven grain boundary segregation (and possibly phase separation) of impurities. This value is relatively high for metals,, and may imply a propensity for localized cohesive failure or fracture at the boundaries. Grain boundary decohesion has been recently shown to occur readily for this alloy due to segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Ni and Mn at elevated temperature, and these failures typically originate along HAGBs and at triple junctions. In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions. This suggests that this alloy may also be prone to grain boundary decohesion without significant segregation and phase separation, i.e., when it is a solid solution.
